newsitem.title: ARMENIA: Rival camps claim victory in Armenia election.
newsitem.headline: Rival camps claim victory in Armenia election.

text.p: Armenian President Levon Ter-Petrosyan's supporters and his main challenger both claimed victory on Monday in a presidential election marred by allegations of fraud.
The Central Election Commission said the 51-year-old president was leading with 56 percent of the votes after more than half the ballot papers were counted from Sunday's election.
His main rival in a field of four, former prime minister Vazgen Manukyan, trailed with 37 percent.

But the returns included only provincial towns and rural areas in the rocky Caucasus state sandwiched between Iran, Georgia, Azerbaijan and Turkey. Figures from the capital Yerevan, Manukyan's main power base, had not yet been announced.
The commission did not say when it would have more complete figures or why counting had been unexpectedly slow.
Ter-Petrosyan issued no statement, but his campaign team said he had won a second five-year term.
"We can already congratulate Levon Ter-Petrosyan as the new president," said Husik Lazaryan, chairman of the Armenian National Movement, which supports him.
But Manukyan, 50, said he was preparing for power and accused Ter-Petrosyan of trying to steal the election.

"We have achieved victory in the first round, regardless of massive falsification. We won't let them have a false president. The people will defend their elections most resolutely," he told a news conference.
Hamlet Gasparyan, press secretary for Ter-Petrosyan's campaign team, dismissed the accusations of major foul play.
"There may have been some violations, but not flagrant ones. It was not enough to change the fact that the president has won," he said.
If a candidate gets more than half the votes cast he wins outright. Otherwise, a runoff between the top two vote-winners will be held in two weeks' time.
Manukyan has promised to revive industry and raise living standards quickly improve in a country which suffered economic collapse after the demise of the Soviet Union in 1991.

Ter-Petrosyan, a aloof academic said by critics to have lost touch with public opinion, made few promises, focusing on stability, recent economic progress and victories over neighbouring Azerbaijan in an eight-year war over territory.
Manukyan and his supporters cried foul even before the polls closed, alleging widespread fraud, intimidation of voters and other irregularities by Ter-Petrosyan's supporters.

International observers have backed up some of the allegations. One said he had seen a large group of soldiers being ordered to vote for Ter-Petrosyan at one polling station, and that the same group then voted again at another location.
He said it was too early to say if the legitimacy of the election was threatened.
Others said that some election officials had attempted to switch ballots or even whole ballot boxes, and that in some locations urns were stolen by Ter-Petrosyan monitors.
One monitor said unregistered voters had been able to vote wherever they wished, raising the prospect of multiple voting.

"In many of the precincts that I saw as many as a quarter of the people who voted were not on the register. This means that if they wanted too, a person could wander around voting as many times as he or she wanted," said Mark Almond, an observer from the British Helsinki Human Rights Group.
"This is clearly against the election code," he said.
